item.title: How Israeli presence in Forest City exposes the Zionist-aligned underbelly of Malaysia. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
How Israeli presence in Forest City exposes the Zionist-aligned underbelly of Malaysia

Submitted by Miriyam Ilavenil on Fri, 07/31/2026 - 09:12
The controversy has fuelled debate over the country's pro-Palestine policy and broader questions about Zionist control
People hold placards and Palestinian flags during a demonstration marking Al-Quds (Jerusalem) Day after Friday prayers in Kuala Lumpur, 13 March 2026 (Mohd Rasfan/AFP)
Off

On 15 July, Anwar Ibrahim, the prime minister of Malaysia, said authorities would deport any Israeli nationals found in the Southeast Asian country, while strongly expressing that Malaysia would "not compromise" on its immigration policies.

"If we find any Israeli, we will deport them immediately because we do not recognise Israel," the prime minister said, according to local media reports.

His comments came as officials investigated allegations that Israelis were involved in a private residential and technology community in the southern state of Johor.

Johor Chief Minister Dato Onn Hafiz Ghazi stated that at the state level, the Iskandar Puteri City Council (MBIP) and relevant agencies would re-examine the Network School's business regulations. 

He also called on the federal bodies of the Home Affairs, Immigration Department, Police and Customs Department to investigate the allegations of Israelis in the Network School. Malaysia's federal Home Affairs Ministry later that day ordered a probe.

After two rounds of investigations, the Immigration Department said there were no violations among the 379 foreign nationals it investigated at the Network School, adding that 19 individuals' movements could not be traced.

The Immigration Department's Director-General Dato Zakaria Shaaban said that these individuals could have entered or left the country illegally. He added that authorities are on the lookout for the untraced individuals.

Then, on 17 July, Ghazi issued several notices to the Network School after authorities found that one of the premises linked to the school was operating without a valid business licence.  

On 23 July, the United States summoned Malaysia's ambassador to the US, Tan Sri Muhammad Shahrul Ikram Yaakob, to explain the nation's position on Israel. The Malaysian government stated that it would not change its immigration stance towards Israel. 

Founder of the Network School, Balaji Srinivasan, announced on X that he wanted an audience with the prime minister to restore his confidence in Malaysia as an investable jurisdiction. 

Balaji Srinivasan: Venture capitalist and Zionist ally

Balaji Srinivasan, a former Silicon Valley venture capitalist and Stanford professor, publicised the Network State in 2022. 

Marketing it vaguely as a startup society focused on peace, Srinivasan proposed building a "startup country" from the internet up. 

The Network State describes the idea on its website as "crowdfunding territory" and "eventually gaining diplomatic recognition from pre-existing states".

Malaysia vows to deport Israelis found in digital nomads community
Read More »

The website calls this new state a composition of an "ethnic diaspora" in which emigrants are connected with "the motherland" and come together in person to build dwellings and structures.

"In a sense, you can think of each physical outpost of this digital community as a cloud embassy," it says, adding that "recruits can visit either the virtual or physical parts of a network state, beta test it, and decide to leave or stay".

Along with Srinivasan, the Network State is financed by tech entrepreneurs Peter Thiel, Marc Andreessen, Joe Lonsdale, Patri Friedman, as well as crypto firms like Coinbase and Praxis.

Peter Thiel's Palantir has invested in Israeli military and surveillance startups accused of providing technological support to Israeli intelligence in the Palestinian genocide.

Praxis, a company funded by Marc Andreessen, Sam Altman and Peter Thiel, has proposed building a tech-owned city on Greenland after US President Donald Trump's repeated threats to take the territory by force. Trump has also shared the intent to build a Trump luxury resort in Gaza.

Critics argue that the Network State model resembles historical settler projects because it envisions digitally organised communities purchasing or controlling physical land.

Some scholars have also pointed to Srinivasan's frequent references to Israel as an example of successful nation-building, arguing that his writings draw inspiration from Israel's state-building experience.

In 2024, centring the pitch around proximity to Singapore, Srinivasan formed the Network School in Malaysia's Forest City, in the southern state of Johor.

Making of Forest City: Fisherfolk and reclaimed land 

The project's location in Malaysia's Forest City in Johor has added another layer of complexity. In a recent video podcast, Srinivasan alludes to the Network School being born out of "nothing into something". 

The "nothing" on which the multibillion-dollar development is built is termed "reclaimed" land in Johor and has faced criticism for its environmental impact on coastal ecosystems and local fishing communities.

Forest City is a joint venture between China's Country Garden Group and Malaysian private company Iskandar Esplanade Danga 88 Sdn Bhd (EDBS), whose shareholders include Johor's Sultan Ibrahim and interests linked to the United Malays National Organisation, a Malay nationalist political party. 

Palestinian engineer 'killed by Mossad' in Malaysia, says family
Read More »

Between July 2024 and June 2025, Malaysia attracted about $759m in data centre investments, with Johor emerging as a key hub alongside the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone. 

An extensive investigation by Mongabay revealed how a Chinese builder began construction in the Forest City without an environmental impact assessment, devastating local seagrass and sparking strong community protests.

The project also saw massive sand dumping, which destroyed marine habitats and hundreds of hectares of traditional fishing grounds. 

Rights groups have previously raised concerns that most of Forest City's workforce comprised low-wage labourers from South Asia, especially Bangladesh. 

The project has drawn controversy again, after allegations circulated online that Israeli nationals were participating in the Network School. 

The dispute exposed contradictions between Malaysia's pro-Palestine foreign policy and its efforts to attract international technology investment, even as government officials have maintained that enforcement actions were based on regulatory compliance rather than political considerations.

Neocolonial Malaysia: US imperial base, pro-Zionist hub 

The developments surrounding the Network School have fuelled a wider debate over Malaysia's balancing of its support for the Palestinian cause and economic relationship with the United States and western capitals.

The country is shaped by a constitutional monarchy, where political and economic power is concentrated among the federal government, state authorities and royal institutions.

Israel condemns Malaysia's decision to bar its athletes from competing
Read More »

The Federation of Malaysia was formed in 1963 and has since come down heavily on the people's movement in Malaya (West Malaysia) and Borneo (East Malaysia), allowing projects like the Network State to be built without much public resistance.

In 2024, Malaysia allowed a subsidiary of BlackRock to join a consortium to take ownership of Malaysia Airports (MAHB), Khazanah Nasional and the Employees Provident Fund (EPF), under the jurisdiction of the finance ministry led by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

Civil society organisations in the country called on Ibrahim to make "the right and conscionable decision" by excluding the "Zionist entity conducting a settler-colonial and racist genocide in Gaza". 

Local media reported that the administration "launched an aggressive media campaign to discredit critics of the plan". 

In April, several international defence companies with business relationships with the Israeli military participated in the Defence Services Asia (DSA) and National Security (Natsec) Asia 2026 exhibition in Kuala Lumpur.

Companies included Lockheed Martin, a US defence contractor that supplies aircraft and other military equipment to Israel, MBDA, a European missile manufacturer whose products have been exported to Israel, and Colt's Manufacturing, a US firearms producer whose weapons are used by the Israeli military. 

Malaysia police free Palestinian kidnapped by Mossad agents: Report
Read More »

Civil society members pointed to investment links between Malaysian conglomerate Sime Darby and Caterpillar, whose bulldozers have been used by the Israeli military in demolitions in the occupied Palestinian territories.

They also cited the operations of Australian rare earths producer Lynas in Malaysia, arguing that rare earth minerals are used in global defence supply chains, including those serving Israel.

Campaigners in Malaysia have alleged that Malaysian ports have been used to facilitate shipments linked to Israel's military supply chain.

In 2025, Ibrahim welcomed Trump during the ASEAN Summit despite protests against his visit.

Police maintained tight security, while rights groups accused Malaysian authorities of detaining and intimidating pro-Palestine protesters during peaceful demonstrations.

While officials have maintained that the country cannot sever ties with every international company that has business links to Israel, the Network School controversy has exposed Malaysia's projection of a pro-Palestine foreign policy alongside its ambition to attract foreign technology investment.

Johor remains a key destination for data centres and AI investments as part of the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone.

Technology
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia

item.title: US to make visa bond programme permanent for people from dozens of countries. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The US State Department will make permanent a visa bond programme that could require applicants from 50 countries, mostly from Africa, to post bonds of up to $20,000 when seeking US visas, according to a federal notice posted online on Friday.

The Federal Register notice applies to B1 and B2 visas, which are issued for business and tourism travel.

“Consular officers may require covered nonimmigrant visa applicants to post a bond of up to $20,000 as a condition of visa issuance, as determined by the consular officers,” the notice said.

“The 2025 visa bond pilot, which provided a framework for the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of the Treasury to assess the feasibility of administering a visa bond programme, has provided sufficient data to suggest that a visa bond programme is an effective tool for enforcing compliance among bonded visa holders.”

In the pilot programme, consular officers could require bonds of $5,000, $10,000 or up to $15,000. The final rule eliminates the $5,000 option and raises the maximum bond to $20,000.

The final rule goes into effect on August 3 when it is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register. In the list of 50 countries for whose citizens this programme applies, 30 are from Africa.

US officials say the policy is intended to reduce visa overstays. Immigration advocates argue it will deter legitimate travel to the United States.

Rights advocates say President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown violates free speech and due process, while creating an unsafe environment for ethnic minorities and encouraging racial profiling. Trump has defended the measures as necessary to bolster national security.

While Trump says he wants to curb illegal immigration, his administration has made legal immigration more difficult, for example, by imposing new and expensive fees for applicants of certain visas and by enforcing social media vetting for applicants and immigrants already in the country.

Earlier in May, the State Department identified nationals from the following 50 countries as being required to post visa bonds: Algeria, Angola, Antigua and Barbuda, Bangladesh, Benin, Bhutan, Botswana, Burundi, Cabo Verde, Cambodia, Central African Republic, Cote D’Ivoire, Cuba, Djibouti, Dominica, Ethiopia, Fiji, Gabon, The Gambia, Georgia, Grenada, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Kyrgyz Republic, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mongolia, Mozambique, Namibia, Nepal, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Papua New Guinea, Sao Tome and Principe, Senegal, Seychelles, Tajikistan, Tanzania, Togo, Tonga, Tunisia, Turkmenistan, Tuvalu, Uganda, Vanuatu, Venezuela, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

item.title: PPP, PML-N continue war of words on eve of Muzaffarabad elections. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The PPP and the PML-N continued lambasting each other on Saturday, extending their rhetoric from the ongoing elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) to the other party’s previous tenures in power.

The PPP and the PML-N — coalition partners in the Centre — have been engaged in a war of words since the PML-N emerged as the winner in the elections in AJK’s Mirpur division. The PPP has accused the PML-N of rigging in Mirpur and demanded re-polling.

The political temperatures remain heated as the second phase of AJK elections is set to be held tomorrow in nine constituencies of Muzaffarabad division. The third phase is scheduled for August 10 in all 12 refugee constituencies, and 11 constituencies of Poonch division.

In the latest exchange, PML-N senior leader Rana Sanaullah questioned the legitimacy of President Asif Ali Zardari’s role as he responded to PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s allegations of rigging in the 2024 general elections.

“If you call the votes secured by the prime minister votes of Forms-47, then on what forms has the president gotten votes on?” Sanaullah said.

On Wednesday, Bilawal had taken a direct jibe at Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, saying: “If someone is sitting on the PM’s seat, or someone is sitting on the CM’s position today, even a child knows that it is not because of the people’s votes or your performance but because of Form-47.”

Sanaullah, also the prime minister’s aide on political affairs and a federal minister, was addressing a gathering in Jhelum Valley alongside Kashmir Affairs Minister Amir Muqam.

Sanaullah further said: “If you say to Mian Nawaz Sharif that he became the prime minister for the first time or every time through rigging, […] then remember, it is also discussed here that someone also became the prime minister for the first time after breaking apart the country.”

He was referring to PPP founder Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who became the president of Pakistan in December 1971 after the secession of Bangladesh (then-East Pakistan) following the 1970 elections.

In August 1973, Bhutto took the oath as the prime minister in 1973 under the new Constitution.

Sanaullah also took a jibe at Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, whose recent remarks have sparked a fresh debate in political circles on the matter of creating new provinces.

Calling Naqvi a “blessed one” of President Zardari, the PML-N leader said the interior minister had “made the [political] journey of 30 years in three-and-a-half years”.

“You began from where and have now reached where, and now you realise that this system is completely dysfunctional.”

In his speech, Muqam criticised the PPP’s governance in Sindh, saying that no performance of the party could be seen.

He also said the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) — a scheme that the PPP often takes credit for launching — was not “anyone’s personal programme but the government’s”.

Earlier on Saturday, PPP leader Saeed Ghani alleged that the PML-N had never won a general election without rigging.

This followed a press briefing by Punjab’s education and sports ministers, where they said that the chief ministers of Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had nothing to show for their performance.

PML-N never won an election without rigging: Ghani

Addressing a press conference in Karachi, Ghani said, “The PPP did not secure power through rigging in any of the elections held till today.

“On the other hand, however many times the PML-N has secured power, it has not been without rigging.”

Ghani, also the Sindh labour minister, made the allegation as he responded to a PML-N member calling on the PPP to not “give lectures on democracy”.

“If you do not want to give the PPP the right to speak on democracy, then will you give it to Gen Musharraf or Gen Zia, or the leaders created by them?” he quipped, referring to the two former military dictators.

The PPP leader said he “did count the 1985 election”, alleging that PML-N supremo and ex-premier Nawaz Sharif “conspired” against ex-prime minister Mohammad Khan Junejo.

He further claimed that his party “became a target of rigging” in the 1988 and 1990 elections, which resulted in the PML-N winning. He went on to allege that the PPP was again “controlled and prevented from forming a government in Punjab” in 1993.

Ghani alleged that the PPP was restricted to “16-17 seats” in the 1997 general elections, when Nawaz’s PML-N again formed the government.

He contended that although the PPP secured power in 2008, the “PML-N was made to win seats, especially in Punjab, through rigging during Musharraf’s tenure”.

Ghani claimed that the PML-N was “made to win” the 2013 elections as well.

“Then the elections in 2024 [took place]. No matter how many times they say, everyone, even children, know that the PML-N was badly defeated in the elections,” he asserted.

The PPP leader alleged that Nawaz, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz “lost their own seats and then blame us”.

Ghani made the remarks after explaining the rationale for his party’s stances on new provinces in Sindh and Punjab, stressing that it was based on the wishes of the people.

He emphasised that the Constitution required any such move to be made through the elected representatives in the provincial assembly concerned.

He noted that the “people of Sindh, its representatives and its assembly say there is no need for further provinces in Sindh”.

On the other hand, Ghani pointed out, the Punjab Assembly and the Senate had passed resolutions over a decade ago calling for two new provinces in Punjab.

“If the people and the elected representatives of Sindh say that there is no need for any new province in Sindh, then no one in Punjab has the right to say whether there should be a new province in Sindh or not,” Ghani asserted.

He went on to stress that the PPP advocated for more provinces in Punjab as the “people of Punjab and their elected representatives” desired that.

The PPP leader emphasised that his party “represented” the citizens of each of the provinces when taking a stance for Sindh and Punjab.

At the outset of his press conference, Ghani also took exception to comments made by “two ministers”, saying it seemed that they “did not know anything about Sindh”.

“They are restricted within a circle called Maryam Nawaz. They only see and say what she tells them, shows them and explains to them,” he said in an apparent reference to the Punjab ministers.

Pakistan pitches textiles amid new US tariffs. [ dawn ]
item.description:
NEW YORK: Pakistan is using one of North America’s largest textile sourcing exhibitions to strengthen its position in the US market as exporters confront new American tariffs and rising production costs amid growing regional competition.

The Pakistan Pavilion at Texworld New York City 2026 opened on Wednesday at the Jacob K. Javits Convention Centre, where five manufacturers are showcasing home textiles, apparel, leather garments, sportswear, gloves and other value-added products for buyers from across the US and overseas.

Organised by the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan (TDAP) in collaboration with the Trade and Investment Wing of Pakistan’s Consulate General in New York, the pavilion showcases A1 Infinity, MRI Group, Hometex Corporation, Ruqi Sports and Niza Sports.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, Pakistan’s Ambassador to the US, Rizwan Saeed Sheikh, described the textile sector as “the backbone of Pakistan’s export economy” and reaffirmed the government’s commitment to expanding exports and to strengthening commercial ties with the US.

10pc duty could cost exporters $2 billion

Textiles and apparel account for the overwhelming majority of Pakis­tan’s exports to the US, while the remainder includes rice, leather products, surgical instruments, sports goods and other manufactured items. Ready-made garments, knitwear and home textiles remain the country’s leading export categories.

Pakistan’s participation comes less than a week after the Office of the US Trade Represen­tative imposed a new 10pc ad valorem tariff on Pakistani imports under Section 301, effective July 24.

The measure followed a US investigation into enforcement of forced-labour import prohibitions in 60 trading partners. While acknowledging that Pakistan legally prohibits forced labour, the USTR said enforcement needed to be streng­­thened, placing the country among those subject to the additional duty.

The tariff follows months of uncertainty over US trade policy. Earlier this year, Wash­ing­ton proposed reciprocal tariffs of up to 29pc on Pakistani goods before negotiations reportedly lowered the baseline rate. Exporters fear that the latest duties, combined with rising domestic production costs, could erode Pakistan’s competitiveness in its most important export market.

Analysts estimate the new tariff could reduce Pakistan’s textile exports by about $564m in FY26, with losses potentially exceeding $2 billion if American buyers shift sourcing to lower-cost suppliers.

Pakistan already faces strong competition from Bangladesh, India, Vietnam and China while domestic manufacturers continue to contend with high energy prices, expensive financing, rising taxes and logistics costs.

Published in Dawn, July 31st, 2026

Litton Das replaces Mehidy Hasan as Bangladesh ODI captain. [ dawn ]
item.description:
DHAKA: Wicket-keeper/batter Litton Das has replaced Mehidy Hasan Miraz as captain of Bangladesh’s One-day International team, the country’s cricket board said on Wednesday.

Mehidy’s captaincy exit comes after Bangladesh ODI series defeat against Zimbabwe earlier this month. Najmul Hossain will continue in his role as Test captain.

The appointment of Litton, who is already the T20 skipper, as the white-ball leader comes as Bangladesh’s move to split captaincy ahead of next year’s ODI World Cup in South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe.

“I and the board believe we should have two captains — a white-ball and a red-ball captain,” Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) president Tamim Iqbal told reporters in Mirpur.

Tamim praised Mehidy’s tenure, which included victories in four of his last five series in charge, but said his dip in batting form prompted the move.

“Mehidy as a cricketer for Bangladesh is more important than anything else…probably the level we’re accustomed to, we’re probably not seeing that right now, especially with his batting,” Tamim said. “I had a discussion with Mehidy, [and] he understands the point.”

Mehidy was handed the ODI captaincy on a 12-month basis in June last year, taking over from Najmul, who had briefly led the side across all formats.

Under Mehidy, Bangladesh won 10 of 20 ODIs, following a difficult start that saw them lose five of their first six matches and drop two consecutive series.

The team later rallied with four straight series wins at home against the West Indies, Pakistan, New Zealand and Australia, before losing an away series to Zimbabwe.

Litton has previous captaincy experience, having led Bangladesh in seven ODIs, including a 2022 series win over India.

Tamim also addressed the uncertain status of Bangladesh’s proposed series against India in September at home.

“I am very hopeful that they will come. Bangladesh is an extremely safe country,” he said.

Tamim said talks with the BCCI had been “very positive” so far and clarity was expected “very soon”.

Under the previous board, Bangladesh refused to play in India at this year’s T20 World Cup, citing security concerns after fast bowler Mustafizur Rahman was dumped by Indian Premier League team Kolkata Knight Riders.

“There are certain things that are beyond my control. They [government] also have to make a decision, I’m sure. Very soon, perhaps, we will find out whether the series is happening or not,” said Tamim.

Published in Dawn, July 30th, 2026

item.title: Hasina vows to return despite fearing for life. [ dawn ]
item.description:
NEW DELHI: Bangladesh’s fugitive ex-premier Sheikh Hasina said she was determined to return to her country by December despite fearing for her life.

“I may be killed. I may be arrested. I may be sent to prison,” Hasina, 78, said in an emailed response to questions by this news agency.

“I am fully aware of my fate. Still, I want to go back because my people are calling me.” Toppled in August 2024 by a student-led uprising that ended her 15-year, iron-fisted rule, Hasina fled by helicopter to India as crowds stormed her palace. The United Nations says up to 1,400 people were killed in crackdowns as she tried to cling to power.

In November, Hasina was found guilty by a Dhaka court of crimes against humanity and sentenced to be hanged — a verdict she described as “political vengeance dressed up as law”.

The former prime minister, who has been living in a secret location in India, insisted there was no pressure for her to return. Relations between India and Bangladesh, strained under the interim administration that took power after Hasina’s fall, have stabilised since Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman took office in February.

Dhaka has formally requested Hasina’s extradition — a request New Delhi has said is “under examination”. Hasina said the issue had “no connection” with her decision to return.

“I can say that I am staying in India with due respect and dignity,” she said. “Indian authorities have not discussed extradition with me. I myself have decided to return to my country.”

The Bangladeshi government has said it will ensure Hasina receives due legal process in all cases against her should she return. Rights groups have long accused Hasina’s former administration of abuses including the murder of rivals, suppression of opposition parties, rigged courts and one-sided elections.

Published in Dawn, July 30th, 2026

item.title: Has the ‘Cockroach’ movement changed Indian politics?. [ chathamhouse ]
item.description:
Has the ‘Cockroach’ movement changed Indian politics? Expert comment jon.wallace 29 July 2026

The movement has tapped into dissatisfaction with employment opportunities and the economy. But it does not threaten a Gen Z revolution of the kind India’s neighbours have undergone.

An Indian youth movement led by an organization calling itself ‘the Cockroach Janata Party’ (CJP) has called a halt to weeks of protest in India, after securing a significant victory: India’s government has acceded to its key demands, and the education minister has resigned.

The rise of the CJP has been remarkable. It began as an online satirical platform, responding to a remark by India’s chief justice in which he referred to the country’s unemployed youth as ‘cockroaches’. But since May it has swiftly developed into a real movement for political and social change, tapping into broader dissatisfaction among India’s young people.

The immediate trigger was a leak in the country’s medical examinations, which over 2.2 million students were due to sit in May. There were reports of several suicides associated with the decision to cancel and then reschedule the exams. The CJP began protests at a site in New Delhi near India’s Parliament, calling for the resignation of the education minister and compensation for affected families. Protests also took hold in other parts of the country.

Movement founder, Abhijit Dipke, returned to India in June to lead the demonstrations. The size of crowds grew from hundreds to thousands after a veteran activist, Sonam Wangchuk, who went on a hunger strike in support of the CJP demonstrations, was forcibly removed from a protest – ostensibly on health grounds. Then heavy-handed tactics by the police against the young protestors went viral, fuelling support for the demonstrations among opposition politicians, celebrities and other sections of Indian society.

With the CJP’s key demands met, the demonstrations have now died down. But the grievances that led to its emergence have not disappeared.

Fundamental grievances remain unresolved

Disaffection among Indian youth reflects structural problems in the economy, including wider flaws in the education system and a lack of employment opportunities.

The exam leak was only the latest in a string of scandals facing the country’s national examination system. Another major leak occurred in 2024. And there have also been leaks of tests for other public service officials, including the police, teachers and engineers.

This points to the need to reform India’s over-centralized examination system, which is overseen by the National Testing Agency, an autonomous body within the Ministry of Education. Education is an emotive issue in India. The country’s middle class spends large proportions of their disposable income on navigating the highly competitive examination system – often through coaching, which is big business in India.

The broader structural problem is the lack of economic opportunity for young people. A third of India’s working age population are aged between 15-29 years. And nearly 40 per cent of school graduates aged between 15-25 years are unemployed.

Related work

South Asia’s Gen Z revolutions now face difficult realities

Even before the latest demonstrations, there were signs of frustration with the government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) performed more poorly than expected in the 2024 general election. 

This was attributed in part to concerns about rising youth unemployment and inequality. The party secured a third consecutive term but on a weaker mandate that made it more beholden to its coalition partners.

These concerns have been exacerbated by the Iran conflict, which is pressuring India’s economy and weakening the Indian Rupee, which is the among the world’s poorest performing currencies.

These economic stresses, combined with flaws in the country’s education system, lie at the heart of India’s youth movement. But this does not mean that India will follow in the footsteps of other countries that have experienced so-called Gen Z revolutions.

Similarities and differences

South Asia has experienced a string of recent ‘people power’ movements. In Sri Lanka in 2022, Bangladesh in 2024 and Nepal in 2025, governments were ousted by largescale social unrest fuelled by growing economic distress, political dysfunction, demographic pressures and the role of social media.

There are clear parallels between these movements and the CJP. India also has a young, aspirational population with grievances over the lack of opportunities. Many feel that the system is inherently unfair, dogged by administrative failures, and unresponsive to their needs. Social media has fuelled their grievances, mobilizing populations and presenting an alternative narrative to the state’s.

However, these comparisons have limitations. India’s youth movement will not unseat the government in the way that it has in neighbouring countries. Despite its name, the CJP is not (yet) a political party, although several opposition politicians are supporting its cause with moral and material support. The group’s objective during the recent demonstrations was quite narrowly defined to reforming the country’s education system.

And the Modi government is on much stronger footing than its peers in neighbouring countries. The BJP has been in power at the national level since 2014. The party and its allies control governments in 22 of India’s 36 states and union territories. There is no strong and unified political opposition. 

That increasingly leaves street movements as the means by which the population voices its opposition to the government – from the farmers’ protests in 2020-21 opposing agricultural law reform, to earlier protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act, which offers fast-track citizenship to minorities from neighbouring countries (but notably not Muslims). Within a day of the CJP calling a halt to its demonstrations, another group – calling itself the E20 Janta Party – was established to oppose the government’s ethanol-blended fuel requirements.

Most of all, grassroots movements face a high barrier to translate their protest support into political power in India, particularly at the national level: Anti-corruption demonstrations in 2011 led to the establishment of the Aam Admi Party (Common Man’s Party). At the time it was seen as a potential third front in Indian politics (after the BJP and Indian National Congress). But today the party only controls one state.

Moreover, despite his strongman image, Modi consistently demonstrates the ability to adapt. After ‘sticks’ failed to quash the CJP protests, his government pivoted to ‘carrots’ – meeting with CJP representatives to hear their demands and censuring several people associated with the exam leak, before dismissing the education minister.

Following an initial period of silence, Modi himself pledged ‘swift and stringent punishment’ for those responsible for the exam paper leaks. A bill was tabled in parliament this week that entails the establishment of fast-track courts to investigate such leaks. And a taskforce led by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani has also been set up to look into the issue. Modi also noted that ‘nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth’.

Outlook

This does not mean that the CJP has not had an impact on India’s politics. The government has been bruised by these demonstrations. As a result, it is more likely to adopt a go-slow approach on some of its more controversial policies, including implementation of a Uniform Civil Code and delimitation of parliamentary constituencies.

And while youth led parties may have a limited impact at the national level, they could have a growing impact at the state level. The Tamil Nadu state election earlier this year saw a relatively new political party (TVK) defeat the state’s well-entrenched political parties with the aid of the youth vote.

By the time of the next general election in 2029 the BJP will have been in power for 15 years, making Modi India’s longest serving prime minister. A degree of Modi fatigue, combined with concerns about the economy and other governance challenges could yet weaken support for the government.

However, as of now it is more likely that movements like the CJP will be a spoiler that erodes the BJP’s mandate, rather than helping to create the kind of cohesive and coordinated opposition required to unseat the government.

item.title: Sindh determined to remove barriers to investment: CM Murad. [ dawn ]
item.description:
KARACHI: Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah on Tuesday pledged immediate resolution of regulatory and operational issues facing British investors and their companies working in the province, assuring the international business community that the government would pursue investor-friendly reforms and policy consistency.

Chairing a high-level Pakistan-UK Roundtable of Multinational Corporations and UK-based firms operating in the province, organised with the British Deputy High Commission, the CM said the government was determined to remove barriers to investment, strengthen public-private engagement and position Sindh as the preferred destination for the foreign investors.

According to a press statement issued by the CM House, the meeting was attended by British Deputy High Commissioner Alison Blackburne, Director Trade Vanessa Montgomery, and representatives of Oxford University Press, Haleon, British International Investment, GSK, Reckitt, Unilever, Standard Chartered Bank, UBL, AstraZeneca and OICCI.

From the Sindh government, Local Government Minister Nasir Hussain Shah, Labour Minister Saeed Ghani, Food Minister Makhdoom Mehboob Zaman, Special Assistant to CM for Investment Syed Qasim Naveed, the chairman of the Sindh Revenue Board and Planning and Development Department, and senior secretaries were present.

“Today’s session was designed with a specific purpose: to listen. I have directed my team to treat these grievances as urgent matters requiring immediate and concrete action,” CM Murad said.

He acknowledged challenges relating to regulatory procedures, taxation, infrastructure, utilities and inter-agency coordination, and stressed that the government would work closely with businesses to remove impediments to growth.

The chief minister said that a government’s primary duty to its investors was to provide stability, transparency and consistency. “We are not only focused on attracting new investment; we are equally committed to ensuring that our existing investors thrive and expand their operations in Sindh,” he said.

CM Murad said the province was simplifying administrative procedures, digitising public services and improving institutional coordination. “We want investors to view us as partners, not merely regulators,” he added.

Special Assistant Syed Qasim Naveed said the government would develop an issue-wise action matrix assigning concerns to relevant departments, with designated focal persons and timelines. “Our objective is to ensure that it leads to clear actions, defined responsibilities and measurable progress,” he said.

Ms Blackburne welcomed the initiative and said the presence of the chief minister signalled Sindh’s commitment to supporting investors.

She said that over 500 reform measures introduced by the provincial government in recent years to reduce regulatory bottlenecks were encouraging for investor confidence.

A presentation by REMIT (Revenue Mobilisation Investment and Trade)/FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office) highlighted that while 74.1 per cent of investors would recommend Pakistan for new FDI (Foreign Direct Investment), 95.1 per cent still perceived business risks as medium to high. Pakistan’s competitiveness score stood at 49.3 out of 100, compared with Bangladesh at 63, Vietnam 71, Indonesia 78, UAE 81, Malaysia 83, India 92 and China 100.

It noted that only 25 of 48 multinational parent companies allocating investment within Asia include Pakistan in their pipeline. Policy predictability, taxation and cost of doing business were identified as the most pressing concerns.

It was informed that Pakistan had implemented 558 reform measures in the past 14 months, generating estimated savings of over Rs468.7 billion for businesses. Seven reform packages had been completed and three more were planned for 2026.

The presentation also noted Sindh’s central role, co-leading reforms in six of 10 major business-environment domains and being directly involved in 259 of 397 high-impact indicators under the World Bank’s B-READY framework.

Concluding the session, representatives of the British International Support Team outlined the evolving UK-Pakistan economic partnership as a journey from strategic priorities and delivery mechanism to measurable outcomes and industry feedback.

Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

item.title: Brigadier held in Bangladesh over staged killing. [ dawn ]
item.description:
DHAKA: An active army officer was detained in Bangladesh on Tuesday over alleged extrajudicial killing of a politician during an anti-narcotics crackdown that left hundreds dead.

Over 460 people were killed during the nationwide anti-drug campaign launched in 2018, according to rights groups, with many deaths alleged to have occurred in staged gunfights involving security forces.

Bangladesh’s crimes tribunal accepted a complaint last week against 11 officials, including former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, a former police chief and six serving and retired military officers, over the killing of Akramul Haque, a councillor in the southeastern district of Cox’s Bazar.

The officer’s detention marks one of the most significant moves yet by the tribunal against those linked to actions taken during Sheikh Hasina’s rule.

“Brig Gen Miftahuddin Ahmed was taken into custody for further judicial proceedings,” army officer Samiud Dowla Chowdhury said.

Chief prosecutor Aminul Islam said investigators had submitted a report detailing the alleged involvement of the accused. The case centres on the killing of Akramul Haque, whom Hasina’s government had described as a “meth kingpin”.

The incident sparked outrage after Haque’s wife, Ayesha Akhter, released an audio recording that she said captured her husband’s final moments and contradicted official claims that he had died in a shootout.

In the recording, Haque can be heard speaking with his wife and children shortly before his death, while his young daughter asks: “Dad, why are you crying?”

Critics alleged at the time that authorities sought to suppress reporting on the case.

“We have been waiting for this day to come for the last eight years,” Akhter said.

“My family and I suffered immense pain, slander, negl­ect and mental distress, but we never lost hope,” she said. “We want to keep faith in our judicial system.”

Published in Dawn, July 29th, 2026

item.title: A Civilizational Reflection on Humanity, Intelligence and the Future of Twenty First Century. [ daily-sun ]
As Myanmar collapses, it’s time for China to step up and be the hero. [ responsiblestatecraft ]
item.description:
The Burmese people continue to suffer as the brutal civil war in Myanmar heads toward its sixth year.

The conflict was recently brought home to America with China’s arrest of Min Zin, an American citizen who heads the Institute for Strategy and Policy (ISP)–Myanmar, located in Thailand. Beijing accused him of spying.

China has increasingly close relations with the government in Naypyidaw, highlighted by the June visit to Beijing of Min Aung Hlaing, the commanding general who recently anointed himself Myanmar’s president. China helps Hlaing’s regime survive despite widespread popular opposition.

For decades the borderlands of Myanmar have been aflame, as ethnic minorities fought for the autonomy promised them when the country gained independence after World War II. The Tatmadaw, or military, seized power in 1962 and has ruled the country in varying iterations ever since. In 2021, Hlaing, disappointed by the hybrid civilian-led government’s refusal to make him president, staged a coup, ending Burma’s brief experiment in limited democratic governance.

In response to widespread protests, the regime "instituted curfews and other limitations on gatherings to curb the demonstrations. Doubling down, the military launched violent campaigns across the country, targeting resistance villages, and silencing and torturing dissenters, displacing thousands in the process,” according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

The junta detained tens of thousands of its citizens as the nation quickly returned to civil war, this time across almost the entire country. Most of Burma now lies beyond the Tatmadaw’s control; the regime is secure only in major cities.

The result is a humanitarian horror. Reports the New York Times: “Far from the spotlight fixed on Iran, Ukraine, Lebanon and other global conflicts, Myanmar, a Southeast Asian nation of about 50 million people, has quietly collapsed.” Tens of thousands have died. Hundreds of thousands have fled the country. Millions have been uprooted. Reports the European Commission: “Mass displacement continues at an alarming rate, with some 3.6 million people displaced as of December 2025, about 90% of whom have been displaced since February 2021.”

The conflict is religious as well. Nearly a decade ago, the military, backed by the civilian authorities, launched a brutal campaign against the largely Muslim Rohingya. As the United Nations’ refugee agency explained, “armed attacks, massive scale violence, and serious human rights violations forced thousands of Rohingya to flee their homes in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Many walked for days through jungles and undertook dangerous sea journeys across the Bay of Bengal to reach safety in Bangladesh,” where roughly a million remain.

Many of the ethnic insurgents — especially the Kachin, Chin, and Karen, as well as smaller shares of the Lahu, Lisu, and Naga — are Christian. Against them the Tatmadaw has promoted Buddhism. Reported the Baltimore Council on Foreign Affairs: “Stated-owned newspapers and television channels report daily about Senior General Min Aung Hlaing and his inner circle making donations to monks, or building monasteries and images of the Buddha.” The regime has demonized religious minorities. According to Georgetown University’s Berkley Center: “the military planted and perpetuated the ideology that to be nationalist is to be Buddhist. … The military successfully used the polarizing ‘us vs. them’ rhetoric in portraying non-Buddhists as threats to the state and in capitalizing Buddhists as protectors of the Burmese race and effective guardians of Buddhism.”

I made my first trip to Karen-held territory more than a quarter century ago and have returned several times since. The region bordering Thailand was long ravaged by conflict, with many Burmese pushed across the border into refugee camps. A tenuous peace was established through a 2012 ceasefire, only to end after the latest coup.

Washington has sanctioned the Tatmadaw and its junta, but Southeast Asia worries little about the nature of ruling regimes. Most important, neither India nor China, competing for influence in Myanmar, is squeamish about working with murderous regimes. Both hosted Hlaing in June, with enhanced economic and security cooperation on the agenda. Analyst Jason Towers noted that Chinese leader “Xi Jinping's frequent meetings and interactions with Min Aung Hlaing since the [2024] Myanmar earthquake send a strong signal that China is supporting his regime at the highest level.” Beijing has pressed insurgents in border territories to end attacks on the regime and the Tatmadaw to safeguard Burma’s natural gas and oil pipelines.

China is the regime’s principal weapons supplier and has blocked proposals for a United Nations arms embargo. Beijing has played a particularly important role in empowering Burma’s air force, which, according to the Special Advisory Council for Myanmar, “has increasingly deployed airstrikes on populated areas, targeting crowded markets, schools, places of worship, camps for internally displaced persons, and hospitals.”

Beijing’s support may have prevented the Tatmadaw’s defeat, but the regime is still unlikely to prevail. It is estimated to control only about one-fifth of the country, half the share held by opposition forces, with the rest of the land contested. According to a Council on Foreign Relations analysis: “The People’s Defense Force (PDF) and its allies continue gaining key territory, pushing the military on the defensive in the Bamar heartland and advancing towards Mandalay. The military junta especially struggles to fight ethnic armed organizations across the country, which have made most of the territorial gains so far.”

Washington’s ability to influence the junta is limited. Economy-wide sanctions targeting the energy industry would injure Burma’s people more than the junta and probably would not crash the regime, given Chinese backing. Washington should do what it can to weaken the Tatmadaw, but that requires cooperating with European governments and especially Burma’s neighbors.

That won’t be easy, since China will remain the most influential foreign actor. The administration should engage Beijing on the issue, seeking to reduce its aid to Naypyidaw. Washington could offer a modus vivendi of sorts, indicating that its primary concern is humanitarian. Thus, Washington could promise to forgo any efforts to court a Burmese government resulting from changed Chinese policy.

An international reform effort led by Xi could better serve Chinese as well as international interests. The Tatmadaw’s ostentatious brutality and corruption ensure continuing conflict, while Beijing’s ability to positively influence events is limited. Cornell University’s Aung Thura Ko Ko observed: “Myanmar is not a chessboard Beijing can fully control. … The greatest long-term risk for China may be anti-China sentiment, which has long existed in Myanmar.”

In contrast, a push for regime change or at least reform, returning basic control to the Burmese people, could better protect Chinese interests. Defusing the conflict would reduce concerns over the security of energy supplies. Ending perceived Chinese support for the junta would relieve popular hostility toward Beijing. Indeed, the civilian regime overthrown by Hlaing had established good relations with its dominant neighbor, and China has maintained contact with opposition forces.

The conflict in Myanmar rarely makes the top of the news in any Western nation. However, it remains one of the world’s worst humanitarian horrors, which President Donald Trump should address. Obviously, Myanmar, under military rule for more than six decades, is a tough case. However, China, despite its official hospitality for Hlaing, should recognize that most of its contacts with Myanmar are about problems, many of them violent. Even for China, a more democratic peace might be a better option than continued unpredictable civil war.

item.title: PTI to move court to get permission for Aug 5 protest. [ dawn ]
item.description:
LAHORE: The Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) leaders have said that they will go to court for its August 5 protest plans as the Lahore deputy commissioner has not responded to their request for permission to hold a peaceful gathering.

This was announced during a press conference of PTI leaders led by Secretary General Salman Akram Raja and PTI Lahore President Mian Akram Usman at the Lahore Press Club on Saturday.

The PTI leaders expressed solidarity with the people of Azad Kashmir, where they said more than 100 people were martyred. “These sacrifices will not go in vain”, the PTI secretary general said. The party leaders condemned the rising incidents of terrorism in Balochistan and recent casualties in District Tank and said that it was a moment of concern for the nation. They accused the state of failing its basic responsibility to protect citizens.

Mr Usman said the party had applied to the Lahore deputy commissioner for permission to hold a peaceful protest but no response had been received so far. “Against this silence, we will go to court and execute our Aug 5 plan,” he asserted.

Says Lahore DC did not respond to its request for permission to hold a peaceful protest

Alleging serious violations in the handling of the Nov 26 incident, Mr Raja said the world saw what happened and that the bodies of PTI martyrs were made to disappear. He claimed the medical reports and bodies of 14 martyrs were ready but relevant people were being threatened.

On economic issues, the PTI leaders criticised the government over wheat and fuel crises and claimed that some 4.5 million tonnes of wheat had gone missing from the country’s total 29 million tonnes. Mr Raja accused the government of “ambushing the public” by increasing petrol, diesel and kerosene prices under the cover of night, calling it a living example of extreme incompetence.

He said that party founder Imran Khan was being held in solitary confinement and denied access to lawyers despite facing 300 cases. “After the 26th Constitutional Amendment, expecting justice from the courts is tantamount to deceiving yourself,” he lamented.

Drawing comparisons with regional movements, he said that just as the youth of India and Bangladesh took to the streets for their rights, Pakistani youth had the same right and should not be underestimated.

“Public movement in the country’s streets on Aug 5 is a call from Imran Khan and his sisters,” he said, and hoped that the nation would come out.

Published in Dawn, July 26th, 2026

Volker Turk's term as UN human rights chief extended despite US warnings. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to renew Volker Turk’s mandate as high commissioner for human rights for four years despite strong opposition from the United States, Russia and Israel.

By a vote of 144 in favour, 10 against, and 13 abstentions, the assembly approved the renewal, beginning October 12, 2026, as proposed by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

An alternative proposal from Russia to extend the mandate by only a few months, until December 31, 2026, was overwhelmingly rejected, as was the US request to postpone the vote.

Ambassador Jeff Bartos, US representative for UN management and reform, criticised the four-year renewal on both procedural and substantive grounds, accusing Guterres of having rushed the process.

“Make no mistake: If this assembly tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals, and the misuse of UN posts, there will be consequences.

“The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding,” he warned just before the vote, accusing Guterres of having rushed the timetable “to hand his long-term friend a four-year executive payout”.

French Ambassador Jerome Bonnafont, however, described Turk as “a voice of conscience” who had demonstrated “rigour and impartiality” during his first term.

Turk, an Austrian jurist, has served as high commissioner since October 2022. He has emphasised the universality of human rights and the need to apply international law equally.

During his tenure, he has been outspoken on the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the war in Gaza, Afghanistan, Sudan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Nicaragua.

But he’s also been criticised for not taking more decisive positions on Cuba, the plight of Uyghurs in Xinjiang, China, and for not directly using the word “genocide” in reference to Gaza, unlike several UN experts and rapporteurs.

Turk’s stances have earned him sharp criticism from several governments, notably Russia and Israel.

Both nations’ ambassadors voiced opposition Friday to his renewal, saying Guterres, whose term as secretary-general expires at the end of the year, should have left the selection of the human rights commissioner to his successor.

item.title: India's 'Cockroach Party' takes aim at Narendra Modi's government after national exam debacle. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
India's 'Cockroach Party' takes aim at Narendra Modi's government after national exam debacle

Submitted by Muheet Ul Islam on Fri, 07/24/2026 - 18:52
Paper Leak sparks student protests as anger mounts against India’s Bharatiya Janata Party
Supporters of India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) hold placards and chant slogans during ongoing protests, days after thousands of protesters marched towards parliament demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, India, on 24 July 2026 (Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters)
Off

Sitting on the ground and beating a tambourine, Arya Singh was surrounded by a large crowd, mostly students, at a square in New Delhi.

“The government that is incompetent must be replaced” and “Long live the revolution”, the voices chanted in unison, led by the 18-year-old Singh.

For nearly a month, students from across the country have been gathering at Jantar Mantar, an 18th-century astronomical observatory and designated street site for protests.

Protesters are demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, a senior leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, and the education minister in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s cabinet. 

The demand comes after the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), one of the world’s largest medical entrance exams, was leaked; it determines admissions into five-year undergraduate medical courses in India.

More than 2.3 million students appeared for the Optical Mark Recognition, or OMR-based exam contesting a total of 137,000 seats on 3 May.

However, an intelligence report about the paper leak through the social media application Telegram in Rajasthan forced authorities to cancel the exam, and a re-examination was held on 21 June.

Between the cancellation and the re-take, at least 12 students were reported to have taken their lives, according to an investigation by Indian Express, which reported that stress, grief and uncertainty led the students to do so. Further self-inflicted deaths have since been reported.

“Those twenty students who committed suicide had given up all outdoor activities, sports, picnics, everything, to prepare for their exams. This is not suicide, it is murder,” Singh told Middle East Eye. 

“If this had happened elsewhere, the minister would have taken responsibility and stepped down. But in India, he continues to hold on to his position without any accountability,” she added.

The ‘Cockroach Party’

The protests have been spearheaded by what is now known as the "Cockroach Janta Party", or CJP. It started as an online movement and satirical gesture after Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, during an open court hearing, said that “parasites” were attacking the system and compared unemployed youth and activists to pests.

“There are youngsters like cockroaches who don’t get any employment or have any place in the profession. Some of them become media, some become social media, RTI activists and other activists, and they start attacking everyone,” Kant said. 

'They call us cockroaches, and maybe we are, because the system is decayed. What else can they expect such a rotten system to produce?'

- Arya Singh, protester

He later backtracked, saying that his remarks referred to individuals with fraudulent degrees and not to India’s youth, whom he called “the pillars of a developed India”.

His comments drew widespread anger, especially among Gen Z, who are dealing with unemployment, rising prices and growing religious divisions and communal violence after 12 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s rule. 

The movement gained further traction after Sonam Wangchuk, a well-known engineer, education reformer and climate activist from Ladakh, joined the protests in support of the CJP by going on a 26-day hunger strike that ended on 24 July.

During the last days of his strike, the 50-year-old was forcibly removed from the protest site by Delhi Police and admitted to a hospital. 

Wangchuk ended his strike after being assured that the police would no longer use force against protesters, that protesters would not face punishment, and that negotiations with the government would continue.

Singh wears the "cockroach" title as a badge of honour.

“They call us cockroaches, and maybe we are, because the system is decayed. What else can they expect such a rotten system to produce?” Singh, the protester, said. 

“The more rotten the system becomes, the more cockroaches it will produce,” she added, saying that this is why they are “out to show what happens when there is no accountability in the government.”

'Brute force'

Abhigyan, 26, a New Delhi resident who goes by one name, has been among the leading faces of the protest. He told MEE that the movement is against corruption, injustice and intolerance, and accused the government of arrogance.

'This is not the response expected from a democratic nation but from a fascist regime' 

- Abhigyan, protester

He said the BJP-led government has used “brute force” against students through lower-level party workers while senior leadership has publicly pushed narratives painting protesters as “anti-national” or as “terrorists”.

“This is not the response expected from a democratic nation but from a fascist regime, and that is what we are witnessing,” Abhigyan said.

Delhi Police, Abhigyan alleges, used sticks with iron nails to beat students, installed iron barricades with an electric current to give shocks, and used pellet guns to disperse the protest when they tried to march towards the Indian parliament on 20 July. 

The Delhi Police, however, in its post on X, termed such reports as “completely false and misleading”.

Abhigyan says there are three confirmed pellet-gun injuries while 65 people were admitted to Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, of which 15 were in critical condition.

“No person in their right mind and with faith in humanity can defend this, unless their employment depends on it or they are simply paid to defend it,” he said, adding that Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah are responsible for escalating the current crisis.

“The protesters did not have the resources to escalate the situation,” he said. 

'What kind of government is this?'

Far away from the main gathering, another group of protesters sat in a circle, reciting a poem: “Paper leak ki sankiya 80 se bhi paar hai, Kaise sarkar hai, Kaise sarkar hai,” which translates to, “Leaked papers have now crossed eighty. What kind of government is this?” 

'BJP is turning the majority of the Indian population, the youth, against them'

- Vijay Ratawal, aspiring doctor and protester

The students were referring to allegations reported in different studies that nearly 70 paper leaks of various exams have taken place in the country during Modi’s tenure.

“The use of force is making us reconsider whether the BJP should remain in power. There were doubts earlier, but now everything has turned black and white: [those] who want to benefit the common people and [those] who only want to hold the most powerful chair in the country,” Vijay Ratawal, a 21-year-old aspiring doctor protesting with the group, told MEE. 

“BJP is turning the majority of the Indian population, the youth, against them,” he said. 

The families of the protesters, Ratawal said, do not trust the system, as they have seen their dreams shatter not only due to exam leaks but also because of the implementation of policies that go against the interests of common citizens.

“The entire BJP cabinet is incompetent; they have set the country on fire on every front,” Ratawal said, citing the farmers’ protests in Gujarat, the violence in Manipur, and the tribal Chita Andolan (funeral pyre protest) in Madhya Pradesh.

“The need of the hour is to ask the BJP regime to step aside and leave the positions they hold to competent people who will serve the country without greed or lust for power,” he said, adding that the silence Modi shows is a lack of commitment to the youth of the country.

Senior citizens like Jankabi Krishnakumar Nirmohi, a 72-year-old farmer from Bhojpur in Bihar, also took part in the protests. He said that his aim was to support the ongoing protests against what he described as the “dictator mindset” of the Modi government.

“In 1974, the Navnirman and JP movements were launched against rampant inflation, food scarcity and government corruption, demanding systemic political change and workers’ rights. The intensity of those protests was much higher than this one, but the cruelty unleashed on students by the BJP government today has no parallel in Indian history,” Nirmohi told MEE. 

“When parliament loses its way, the streets begin to speak, and that is when decisions are made,” he said.

“The shamelessness of Modi can be seen in his post on X, in which he praised the education minister on his birthday while students were protesting against him,” Nirmohi said. 

“He did not even mourn the loss of the 20 students who died by suicide. The greetings and the blessing wishes show clearly where his support lies,” he concluded.

Gen Z battleground

South Asia in recent years has become a battleground for Gen Z-led protests, resulting in governments being toppled in countries like Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh. 

Sanjay Kumar, an Indian political scientist, psephologist and professor at the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies, or CSDS, told MEE that the youth have sent a clear signal of their unhappiness with the BJP government. 

However, he expressed scepticism about the extent to which the movement can sustain itself.

'When Parliament loses its way, the streets begin to speak, and that is when decisions are made'

- Sanjay Kumar, political scientist

“Yes, the protest is a clear indication that there is unhappiness among the youth against the current government, especially with regard to the NEET paper leak,” Kumar said, adding that opposition leaders also visited the protests in solidarity.

Kumar said he cannot confirm whether the protests were being organised by opposition political parties, as reported by sections of the Indian national media.

“My assessment is that it was neither started nor organised by opposition parties,” Kumar said. “However, once the movement began, [the] opposition saw it as an opportunity and tried to take advantage of it by sending a message to the youth that they are the ones looking after their interests.” 

But Kumar does not see a direct parallel between what is happening in New Delhi and the events that took place in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal.

“It is not useful to make such comparisons, because those are smaller countries, and something happening in the capital here has very different implications for the country,” Kumar said, 

“If you speak to people in rural areas, which make up nearly 70 percent of the population, I do not think this movement will have much resonance. The momentum is issue-specific and limited to a particular section of the population, mainly the youth of the country,” he added.

Noor Ahmad Baba, a political scientist and former professor at the University of Kashmir, believes that the BJP has not asked for the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister, because the government does not want to show any signs of weakness.

Meanwhile, Dharmendra Pradhan accused the Indian National Congress (INC), the main opposition party, of using students as political tools and disrupting the Monsoon Session of Parliament.

“Even after the government conveyed its readiness for a comprehensive discussion, the Congress chose political spectacle over democratic debate. Their objective was never solutions for students; it was disruption for political headlines,” he said in a post on X. 

“The students of India deserve far better than being treated as tools in a political campaign. They deserve certainty over chaos, solutions over slogans and responsibility over disruption,” Pradhan added. “We owe our students more than outrage. We owe them answers, reforms and accountability. That is exactly what our government remains committed to delivering,” he said.

But Baba says the government has not faced a challenge like this before and “it does not want to show any sign of weakness by asking for Pradhan’s resignation”.

“It will be interesting to see how the BJP handles this situation,” he added, saying that “having no precedent in the past does not necessarily ensure that a new precedent can’t be created.”

Academic Freedom
New Delhi
